Given a list of integers, write a Python function that returns the first number that appears only once, or None if there isn't one. Example: [4, 2, 4, 5, 2, 3] returns 5. Talk me through your approach before writing code, including its time and space complexity.

That's the right approach: counting first, then scanning the original list preserves which unique number comes first. Assuming the emoji replaced "(n)", O(n) time and O(n) extra space are right under average-case dictionary operations. Can you write the function now, including what it returns for an empty list?

It returns 5 for the example, but an empty list or a list with no unique number raises StopIteration instead of returning None. Use next((n for n in nums if counts[n] == 1), None), and replace the list comprehension with a normal counting loop so you don't build an unused list. Follow-up: if the input is a generator you can only traverse once, how would you adapt your approach?

I'd compare what you can save after taxes, your actual rent, commuting and benefits, rather than the headline salaries. If the teams and growth prospects are truly equal, I'd lean Chicago unless the NYC budget still supports your savings goals or you genuinely want the experience of living there. But "same kind of role" isn't necessarily the same opportunity: manager quality, responsibility and where people land next could matter more than the salary gap.

From your resume and what you've told me, I remember these roles: • Pixelforge founder, 2023-2025: 70+ hand-coded React sites and peak $9k monthly recurring revenue, per your resume • Rallyup co-founder: youth-sports management software, customer discovery with coaches/trainers, and paying teams; your November update mentioned Northside Athletics and Prime Court Athletics • Waypoint solo founder, part-time: career agent covering applications, resumes, research and networking; I'm not treating planned features as proven results • Harbor Global: AI M&A / technology investment-banking internship • Crestline Partners / Crestline Search Partners: private-equity internship, listed as 2025 on your resume • Mindgrove AI Research: research on AI continuity and memory, listed since August 2026 • Elmstead: GTM team, listed since September 2026 • Ondo / Loop: founder work on an AI voice ring and agent software, including manufacturer sourcing Related leadership: Sigma Tau historian, plus Lakeshore investing/finance clubs. The gaps I'd flag before reusing any of this are conflicting Harbor dates, Crestline's exact company name, changing Rallyup revenue figures, and detailed responsibilities/results for Harbor, Crestline and Elmstead.

Pay: Citadel's official university-graduate SWE posting lists $235k-$300k base plus a discretionary bonus, not guaranteed total compensation. It currently lists New York, Miami, Greenwich and Houston, not Chicago.
https://www.citadel.com/careers/details/software-engineer-university-graduate-us/

Interviews: Citadel describes a 45-minute first round, a second round with three 45-minute interviews, then team matching, with the overall process taking roughly eight weeks. Expect coding and behavioral questions; candidate accounts also describe an online assessment, but I wouldn't assume every candidate gets an identical sequence.
https://www.citadel.com/careers/career-perspectives/our-engineering-interview-process/

Culture: my read is high upside with a real pressure risk, so I'd interview the manager as hard as they interview you. Anonymous accounts describe demanding hours and performance pressure, but they're anecdotes, not proof every team operates that way. Ask about normal hours, on-call, turnover and what happens when someone misses expectations.
https://www.reddit.com/r/quant/comments/10d7lv1/why_do_people_say_citadel_has_bad_wlb/

One important distinction: Citadel and Citadel Securities are different employers, so don't mix their offer numbers or team reputations. This reporting explains the engineering differences, though it's from 2022 rather than a current culture audit.

In that situation, I'd build the resume around one or two projects you can demo and defend technically, leave GPA off unless required, and never disguise projects as employment. I'd combine targeted applications with short, specific outreach to alumni and engineers, including smaller companies and software teams outside big tech rather than betting everything on famous new-grad programs. Track where you lose people: no screens means revisit targeting and resume evidence; screens without offers means work on interview performance, not just send more applications.

Right now that's a plot summary, not an interview answer: "they didn't like it, I redid it, I communicated better" gives me no evidence of ownership or change. The client disliking it isn't necessarily your failure; what did YOU get wrong, what did redoing it cost, and what specific step did you change afterward? Start with what the client expected versus what you delivered, using only what actually happened.
